title: Stoned at Ta'if
hook: he walks to Ta'if to seek help, and is mocked and driven out

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Talib dies. Your line was: the shield is gone. Did your thanks reach the person who protected you? Day seven hundred fifty.

Mecca has closed its doors. The wife who held him is buried. The uncle who shielded him is buried. So he does something that takes nerve: he leaves, on foot, for Ta'if, a town in the hills, to ask its tribe, Thaqif, for help and a hearing. No army, no escort of clan, no promise of welcome. He's going to knock on the door of strangers and say what he has said in Mecca. Today: what happened when he got there. Stoned at Ta'if.
screen: `MECCA HAS CLOSED.` → `ON FOOT TO THE HILLS.` → `KNOCKING ON STRANGERS' DOORS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says he went to the leaders of Thaqif, three brothers, and sat with them and told them why he'd come. Ibn Ishaq keeps their answers, and they are sharp. One says, in effect, if God sent you, I'll tear the covering of the Ka'ba. Another says: couldn't God find anyone but you to send? The third says: I won't speak to you at all. If you're really a messenger, you're too great for me to answer, and if you're lying, you're not worth answering. Three doors, shut. He gets up and asks them one thing: then keep this between us. They don't. They stir up the people of the town, and, as the accounts tell it, a crowd follows him out, jeering and shouting, and in some tellings throwing stones, until he reaches an orchard outside town and takes shelter by its wall. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps his own words about a day like this, years later. Aisha asks him whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says the worst was the day of al-Aqabah, when he offered himself to Ibn Abd Yalil and was turned away; commentators connect that day with Ta'if. He says he went off with his grief, not knowing where he was going, and didn't come to himself until he'd reached a place called Qarn al-Tha'alib. The man Muslims honor as the final messenger tells his wife that he walked in a daze, not seeing the road. The story doesn't hide it. But notice the verb. He went. He didn't stay in the orchard, and he didn't stay in Ta'if. Hurt and dazed, he kept walking. What he said and met along that road is the next few days.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS, THREE NOS.` · `KEEP THIS BETWEEN US.` · `A CROWD, AND STONES.` · `HE WALKED IN A DAZE.` · then, large: `HE KEPT WALKING.`

segments.voice: The practice: walk on after rejection. If you can, stand up. Bring to mind one no you've been given lately: a job, an application, an apology not accepted, a message left on read. Don't argue with it. Let it be as heavy as it is. Then take a few slow steps, wherever you are, across the room, down the hall. Feel each foot land. You don't have to feel better to take the next step. If you can't walk right now, press each foot into the floor in turn. If you pray, you can bring that no to Allah as it is. The bell holds the time.
Stoned at Ta'if. He went to Thaqif for help, was turned away, mocked and driven out, and kept walking. Today's word.
Your line: he walked on. Today, after the next no you hear, big or small, take one concrete next step within the hour. Day seven hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the journey to Ta'if as part of the Meccan sirah, retold just before the night journey, and it is remembered when people face rejection.

fork.setup: you're him. three leaders have refused you, one with an insult. before you leave, what do you ask?
options: that they at least hear one more argument.
that they keep this between you.
that they give you food for the road.
fork.reveal: Ibn Ishaq says he asked them to keep it quiet. they told the town instead.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the hill town of Thaqif, in the mountains near Mecca.

trapdoor: what you thought: he was simply chased out of a town.
what it means: after losing his shield, he went to strangers, was refused and mocked, and kept walking.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's three brothers of Thaqif, and Bukhari's report naming Ibn Abd Yalil and the walk to Qarn al-Tha'alib.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the journey to Ta'if; the three brothers of Thaqif and their replies; the request for secrecy; the crowd; the orchard)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 (Aisha asks of a day harder than Uhud; Ibn Abd Yalil; he walked in grief until Qarn al-Tha'alib)

notes: Index hook says 'mocked and stoned out'; Ibn Ishaq's text as recalled speaks of louts and slaves insulting him and crying after him; the stones come from other accounts. Script says 'as the accounts tell it'. Confirm.
The three brothers' replies are paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm.

Bukhari 3231 places this 'the day of Aqabah' with Ibn Abd Yalil ibn Abd Kulal; commentators link it to Ta'if. Confirm the link is fair, and that tomorrow's/day 753's use of the same hadith doesn't overlap too much.
'The man Muslims honor as the final messenger' is a description of Muslim belief, not a claim by the narrator; confirm it reads that way.
Hook description of Ta'if as 'a town in the hills' and the original note 'in the mountains near Mecca' are geographic generalities; confirm.

Editor pass: stones softened to 'in some tellings' (Ibn Ishaq as cited speaks of insults and jeering); aligned Bukhari 3231's answer ('the hardest was the day...'); cut 'often' from howItsDone and a stock 'sit with that'.

Audit pass (serious): removed the narrator's historicity judgment ('almost too sharp to be invented'); Bukhari 3231 names 'the day of al-Aqabah', not Ta'if, so the teach now says so and attributes the Ta'if link to commentators.
